newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Chan says PNG may drop mercenaries after protests.
newsitem.headline: Chan says PNG may drop mercenaries after protests.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Wednesday offered an olive branch to rebel army officers, saying his government would consider dropping a plan to use mercenaries on Bougainville island.

Chan's comments came after a fresh challenge to his authority on Wednesday as army officers rallied against the use of mercenaries to quell a nine-year island uprising on Bougainville and a street protest erupted in violence.

Chan said he was in complete control of the South Pacific nation, which was thrown into chaos when he sacked the country's army chief who had demanded Chan's resignation over plans to use the mercenaries against seccessionist rebels on Bougainville.

Protesters on Wednesday delivered a petition which called for the mercenaries to be sent home and for Chan to resign. Chan said six of the 40 mercenaries hired by British-based Sandline International left the country on Wednesday. The other 34 remained confined to barracks in the north of the country.
"The cancellation of Sandline, as demanded by the petition, will be considered by the cabinet," Chan told a news conference. "But we must not be too premature about making that decision.
"The security aspects of the engagement...have been compromised by the publicity," he said.

Former army chief Jerry Singirok said on Tuesday he accepted his dismissal but remained holed up in Port Moresby's main barracks, where at least 1,500 protesters arrived to back him in his campaign against Chan.
Major Walter Enuma said before the protests the defence force still considered Singirok to be its commander and demanded that all the mercenaries leave.

"The mercenaries have come in here and undermined the constitutional rule of this country," Enuma, a handgun in one hand and loud-hailer in the other, told cheering protesters outside the city's Murray barracks.
Chan said he would not resign and added acting commander Colonel Alfred Aikung was in charge of the Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) despite the apparent split in the army.
"The question of resignation -- you can forget about that," he said.
"I'm satisfied that the (acting) commander is in full control."
Protesters had earlier tried to entice soldiers to join them in a march on parliament house but the soldiers cheered them while remaining in barracks.
Violence followed within hours when demonstrators broke loose from the crowd and started looting nearby shops.
"Unfortunately some looters have taken advantage of the situation and some of our shops have been raided," Chan said.
In a first wave, about 200 demonstrators broke loose and attacked two supermarkets. Police fired tear gas into the crowd and live ammunition over their heads to calm the situation.
The demonstration officially dispersed after the petition was handed to a government minister.

But the bulk of the protesters, many of them laughing, ran up a main city street to loot another supermarket. Heavily-armed police fired teargas and more live rounds at the looters, who dispersed within 30 minutes.
Chan has been criticised internationally over the mercenary plan for resource-rich Bougainville island, 900 km (560 miles) northeast of the capital.
Australia, one of the leading critics, on Wednesday sent a diplomatic mission to Port Moresby to help end the crisis.
